cards.front: Complete: Marina _____ (drink) an espresso every morning before work.
cards.back: Marina drinks an espresso every morning before work.
cards.meaning: Simple present describes a repeated habit.
cards.example: The café opens at seven and closes at nine.

cards.front: Fill in: This restaurant _____ (not/serve) meat on Mondays.
cards.back: This restaurant doesn't serve meat on Mondays.
cards.meaning: General facts and fixed rules use simple present.
cards.example: The kitchen closes orders at eleven.

cards.front: Fill in: The flight to São Paulo _____ (leave) at 6:40 every day.
cards.back: The flight to São Paulo leaves at 6:40 every day.
cards.meaning: Timetables and schedules use simple present even for future events.
cards.example: The train departs from platform 4 at nine.

cards.front: Fill in: Our team _____ (meet) every Monday to review the sprint.
cards.back: Our team meets every Monday to review the sprint.
cards.meaning: Routine at work is expressed with simple present.
cards.example: The manager sends the report on Fridays.

cards.front: Fill in: This store _____ (accept) returns within thirty days.
cards.back: This store accepts returns within thirty days.
cards.meaning: Store policies are general facts, so simple present is used.
cards.example: They exchange defective items for free.

cards.front: Fill in: Dr. Alves _____ (see) patients on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
cards.back: Dr. Alves sees patients on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
cards.meaning: A fixed schedule is a routine fact.
cards.example: The clinic opens at eight in the morning.

cards.front: Fill in: Rafael _____ (do) the dishes every night after dinner.
cards.back: Rafael does the dishes every night after dinner.
cards.meaning: A repeated household habit uses simple present.
cards.example: She waters the plants twice a week.

cards.front: Fill in: We usually _____ (get) together on Saturday nights.
cards.back: We usually get together on Saturday nights.
cards.meaning: A habitual social activity uses simple present.
cards.example: They play cards every Friday.

cards.front: Fill in: The bank _____ (charge) a fee for international transfers.
cards.back: The bank charges a fee for international transfers.
cards.meaning: A general policy or fact takes simple present.
cards.example: This account earns interest monthly.

cards.front: Fill in: My phone _____ (update) itself automatically at night.
cards.back: My phone updates itself automatically at night.
cards.meaning: A regular automatic action is expressed with simple present.
cards.example: The app syncs data every hour.

cards.front: Fill in: I can't talk now — I _____ (order) coffee for the whole team.
cards.back: I can't talk now — I'm ordering coffee for the whole team.
cards.meaning: An action happening right now uses present continuous.
cards.example: She's making a cappuccino for the customer.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (meet) Carla for dinner at that new sushi place on Friday.
cards.back: We're meeting Carla for dinner at that new sushi place on Friday.
cards.meaning: A fixed future arrangement uses present continuous.
cards.example: They're having lunch with a client tomorrow.

cards.front: Translate: 'Estou fazendo as malas para a viagem.'
cards.back: I'm packing my bags for the trip.
cards.meaning: An action in progress right now uses present continuous.
cards.example: He's checking in for his flight right now.

cards.front: Fill in: Bruno _____ (prepare) the slides for tomorrow's presentation.
cards.back: Bruno is preparing the slides for tomorrow's presentation.
cards.meaning: An ongoing task at the moment of speaking is present continuous.
cards.example: They're reviewing the budget this week.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (look) for a birthday gift for my sister.
cards.back: I'm looking for a birthday gift for my sister.
cards.meaning: A current, temporary activity uses present continuous.
cards.example: She's trying on shoes right now.

cards.front: Fill in: The nurse _____ (take) your blood pressure now.
cards.back: The nurse is taking your blood pressure now.
cards.meaning: An action in progress at this moment uses present continuous.
cards.example: The doctor is examining another patient.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (repaint) the kitchen this weekend.
cards.back: We're repainting the kitchen this weekend.
cards.meaning: A planned, arranged action uses present continuous for the near future.
cards.example: He's fixing the leaking faucet tonight.

cards.front: Fill in: Ana and Paulo _____ (throw) a party next Saturday.
cards.back: Ana and Paulo are throwing a party next Saturday.
cards.meaning: A definite personal arrangement uses present continuous for future plans.
cards.example: We're visiting my parents next weekend.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (transfer) the money right now, just a second.
cards.back: I'm transferring the money right now, just a second.
cards.meaning: An action happening at the moment of speaking uses present continuous.
cards.example: The bank is updating its app this week.

cards.front: Fill in: Why _____ (you/call) me from an unknown number?
cards.back: Why are you calling me from an unknown number?
cards.meaning: A present action in progress is questioned with present continuous.
cards.example: She's texting her boss about the delay.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (order) a latte, but they gave me a cappuccino.
cards.back: I ordered a latte, but they gave me a cappuccino.
cards.meaning: A finished action at a specific past moment uses simple past.
cards.example: She paid with a card yesterday.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (eat) at that new Thai place last night.
cards.back: We ate at that new Thai place last night.
cards.meaning: A completed action in the past uses simple past.
cards.example: He tried the seafood pasta last week.

cards.front: Fill in: Our flight _____ (land) two hours late yesterday.
cards.back: Our flight landed two hours late yesterday.
cards.meaning: A finished event tied to a past time uses simple past.
cards.example: They lost their luggage in Frankfurt last month.

cards.front: Fill in: Juliana _____ (send) the report before she left the office.
cards.back: Juliana sent the report before she left the office.
cards.meaning: Both actions are finished past events in sequence, so simple past is used.
cards.example: He finished the project on Tuesday.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (return) the shoes because they didn't fit.
cards.back: I returned the shoes because they didn't fit.
cards.meaning: A completed action with a clear past time context uses simple past.
cards.example: She bought a new jacket last weekend.

cards.front: Fill in: The doctor _____ (prescribe) antibiotics last time I was sick.
cards.back: The doctor prescribed antibiotics last time I was sick.
cards.meaning: A finished past medical event uses simple past.
cards.example: I broke my arm two years ago.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (clean) the whole apartment on Sunday.
cards.back: We cleaned the whole apartment on Sunday.
cards.meaning: A completed household task in the past uses simple past.
cards.example: He fixed the shower yesterday.

cards.front: Fill in: They _____ (cancel) the barbecue because of the rain.
cards.back: They cancelled the barbecue because of the rain.
cards.meaning: A finished past event uses simple past.
cards.example: We celebrated her birthday last Saturday.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (open) a savings account when I moved to Canada.
cards.back: I opened a savings account when I moved to Canada.
cards.meaning: A specific completed past action uses simple past.
cards.example: The bank charged an extra fee last month.

cards.front: Fill in: My phone _____ (die) right in the middle of the call.
cards.back: My phone died right in the middle of the call.
cards.meaning: A finished past action at a specific moment uses simple past.
cards.example: She dropped her phone in the sink last week.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (wait) for my coffee when I saw an old friend.
cards.back: I was waiting for my coffee when I saw an old friend.
cards.meaning: Past continuous sets the background action interrupted by a simple past event.
cards.example: She was reading the menu when the waiter arrived.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (have) dinner when the power went out.
cards.back: We were having dinner when the power went out.
cards.meaning: An action in progress in the past, interrupted by another action.
cards.example: They were ordering dessert when the fire alarm rang.

cards.front: Fill in: While we _____ (board) the plane, my phone rang.
cards.back: While we were boarding the plane, my phone rang.
cards.meaning: A background ongoing action in the past uses past continuous.
cards.example: He was checking his passport when the gate closed.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (write) an email when the client called.
cards.back: I was writing an email when the client called.
cards.meaning: An interrupted ongoing action in the past requires past continuous.
cards.example: She was presenting the slides when the projector broke.

cards.front: Fill in: While I _____ (try) on jeans, the fire alarm went off.
cards.back: While I was trying on jeans, the fire alarm went off.
cards.meaning: Background action interrupted by a sudden past event.
cards.example: He was paying at the register when his card was declined.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (feel) dizzy while I was waiting for the exam results.
cards.back: I was feeling dizzy while I was waiting for the exam results.
cards.meaning: An ongoing state around a specific past time uses past continuous.
cards.example: She was coughing badly when the doctor walked in.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (paint) the fence when it started to rain.
cards.back: We were painting the fence when it started to rain.
cards.meaning: Interrupted ongoing action in the past.
cards.example: He was fixing the sink when the water pipe burst.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (talk) to Bianca when you texted me.
cards.back: I was talking to Bianca when you texted me.
cards.meaning: Background action interrupted by another past event.
cards.example: They were dancing when the music suddenly stopped.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (fill) out the loan form when the system crashed.
cards.back: I was filling out the loan form when the system crashed.
cards.meaning: An action in progress interrupted by another past event.
cards.example: She was checking her balance when the app froze.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (text) my sister when the battery died.
cards.back: I was texting my sister when the battery died.
cards.meaning: Ongoing past action interrupted by a sudden event.
cards.example: He was video calling his mom when the wifi went down.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (never/try) oat milk in my coffee — is it good?
cards.back: I've never tried oat milk in my coffee — is it good?
cards.meaning: Life experience up to now, with no specific finished time, uses present perfect, not simple past.
cards.example: She has already tasted every flavor on the menu.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I have eaten sushi yesterday.'
cards.back: I ate sushi yesterday.
cards.meaning: A specific finished past time ('yesterday') requires simple past, not present perfect — a common error for Portuguese speakers.
cards.example: We went to that restaurant last week.

cards.front: Fill in: _____ (you/ever/be) to Lisbon?
cards.back: Have you ever been to Lisbon?
cards.meaning: Asking about life experience up to now, without a specific time, uses present perfect.
cards.example: I have never visited Japan.

cards.front: Translate: 'Já enviei o relatório.' (said this morning, still relevant now)
cards.back: I have already sent the report.
cards.meaning: The action is finished but its result matters right now, so present perfect is used, not simple past as Portuguese would suggest.
cards.example: She has already finished the presentation.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (just/buy) this jacket — do you like it?
cards.back: I've just bought this jacket — do you like it?
cards.meaning: 'Just' signals a very recent action with present relevance, requiring present perfect.
cards.example: They have just opened a new store downtown.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I have seen the doctor two days ago.'
cards.back: I saw the doctor two days ago.
cards.meaning: A definite past time ('two days ago') needs simple past, not present perfect.
cards.example: I had my checkup last Tuesday.

cards.front: Fill in: Someone _____ (break) the window — look!
cards.back: Someone has broken the window — look!
cards.meaning: The action's result is visible now, so present perfect connects past and present.
cards.example: She has already cleaned the whole house.

cards.front: Fill in: _____ (you/hear) the news about Camila's wedding?
cards.back: Have you heard the news about Camila's wedding?
cards.meaning: News with present relevance and no specific past time uses present perfect.
cards.example: I haven't seen Diego since college.

cards.front: Translate: 'Eu abri uma conta essa manhã.' (still today, morning not over)
cards.back: I have opened an account this morning.
cards.meaning: 'This morning' as an unfinished time period requires present perfect if the period is still current.
cards.example: We have already paid this month's bill.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I didn't receive your message yet.'
cards.back: I haven't received your message yet.
cards.meaning: 'Yet' with an unfinished situation up to now requires present perfect, not simple past.
cards.example: She hasn't replied to my email yet.

cards.front: Which tense describes something that happened at an unspecified past time, with a result relevant today?
cards.back: Present perfect — e.g., 'I have already had two coffees today.'
cards.meaning: Present perfect links a past action to the present moment.
cards.example: He has finished his coffee already.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (never/order) delivery from that place before.
cards.back: We've never ordered delivery from that place before.
cards.meaning: Experience up to now with no specific time uses present perfect.
cards.example: I haven't tried the vegan menu yet.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I have lost my passport last week.'
cards.back: I lost my passport last week.
cards.meaning: 'Last week' is a specific finished time, so simple past is correct, not present perfect.
cards.example: We arrived in Berlin three days ago.

cards.front: Fill in: Our team _____ (already/finish) the quarterly review.
cards.back: Our team has already finished the quarterly review.
cards.meaning: A completed action relevant to the current situation at work uses present perfect.
cards.example: The manager has approved the new budget.

cards.front: Translate: 'Comprei esse tênis semana passada.'
cards.back: I bought these sneakers last week.
cards.meaning: A specific past time ('semana passada') requires simple past in English.
cards.example: She purchased a new laptop two months ago.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (have) this headache since this morning.
cards.back: I've had this headache since this morning.
cards.meaning: An unfinished period ('since this morning') connecting past to present uses present perfect.
cards.example: She has felt tired for the last few days.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I cleaned the kitchen already.' (just now, relevant now)
cards.back: I have already cleaned the kitchen.
cards.meaning: 'Already' with present relevance calls for present perfect rather than simple past.
cards.example: He has already fixed the leaking tap.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (know) each other for over ten years.
cards.back: We've known each other for over ten years.
cards.meaning: A state that started in the past and continues now uses present perfect with 'for'.
cards.example: They have been friends since high school.

cards.front: Fill in: The bank _____ (not/respond) to my complaint yet.
cards.back: The bank hasn't responded to my complaint yet.
cards.meaning: An unfinished situation up to now uses present perfect, not simple past.
cards.example: I haven't received the refund yet.

cards.front: Translate: 'Ele me ligou hoje de manhã.' (morning is over, it's now afternoon)
cards.back: He called me this morning.
cards.meaning: Once the time period is finished (the morning has passed), simple past is used instead of present perfect.
cards.example: She texted me an hour ago.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (work) at this café since I moved to Dublin.
cards.back: I've been working at this café since I moved to Dublin.
cards.meaning: An ongoing action that started in the past and continues now uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: She has been studying English for six months.

cards.front: Fill in: They _____ (wait) for a table for twenty minutes.
cards.back: They've been waiting for a table for twenty minutes.
cards.meaning: Emphasis on the duration of an ongoing action uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: We've been standing in line since noon.

cards.front: Translate: 'Estamos viajando pela Europa há três semanas.'
cards.back: We've been traveling around Europe for three weeks.
cards.meaning: This ongoing-duration structure has no direct Portuguese equivalent and requires present perfect continuous.
cards.example: He's been backpacking through Asia for two months.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (prepare) this proposal all week.
cards.back: I've been preparing this proposal all week.
cards.meaning: An activity in progress over a recent period, with emphasis on duration, uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: She's been answering emails since 8 a.m.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (look) for a new mattress for weeks now.
cards.back: I've been looking for a new mattress for weeks now.
cards.meaning: An unfinished search over time emphasizes duration with present perfect continuous.
cards.example: They've been comparing prices online all day.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (feel) dizzy for the past three days.
cards.back: I've been feeling dizzy for the past three days.
cards.meaning: A continuing symptom emphasizes duration up to now, using present perfect continuous.
cards.example: She's been coughing since last weekend.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (renovate) the bathroom for over a month.
cards.back: We've been renovating the bathroom for over a month.
cards.meaning: An ongoing project with emphasis on how long it has taken uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: He's been fixing that car for weeks.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (plan) this trip since January.
cards.back: I've been planning this trip since January.
cards.meaning: An ongoing action started in the past, still relevant, focuses on duration.
cards.example: They've been organizing the reunion for months.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (try) to reach customer service all morning.
cards.back: I've been trying to reach customer service all morning.
cards.meaning: Repeated or continuous effort over a period uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: She's been disputing the charge for a week.

cards.front: Fill in: My phone _____ (overheat) a lot lately.
cards.back: My phone has been overheating a lot lately.
cards.meaning: A recurring, ongoing recent problem uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: The app has been crashing all day.

cards.front: Which tense emphasizes the DURATION of an unfinished action up to now?
cards.back: Present perfect continuous — e.g., 'I've been standing in this line for ten minutes.'
cards.meaning: This tense highlights how long something has been happening, not just that it happened.
cards.example: He's been roasting his own coffee beans for years.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I am waiting for this table for half an hour.'
cards.back: I've been waiting for this table for half an hour.
cards.meaning: Duration up to now, an unfinished action, needs present perfect continuous, not present continuous.
cards.example: We've been standing outside since it started raining.

cards.front: Fill in: The airline _____ (delay) our flight all day.
cards.back: The airline has been delaying our flight all day.
cards.meaning: A repeated, ongoing situation with visible present effect uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: We've been checking the departure board every hour.

cards.front: Translate: 'Estou tentando ligar para o cliente a manhã toda.'
cards.back: I've been trying to call the client all morning.
cards.meaning: Continued effort over a period, still ongoing, needs present perfect continuous.
cards.example: She's been drafting that contract since Monday.

cards.front: Fill in: How long _____ (you/save) for this TV?
cards.back: How long have you been saving for this TV?
cards.meaning: Asking about duration of an ongoing action uses present perfect continuous.
cards.example: I've been collecting coupons for this sale for weeks.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (take) these pills for two weeks and I still feel sick.
cards.back: I've been taking these pills for two weeks and I still feel sick.
cards.meaning: An ongoing treatment with a duration, and present relevance (still sick), needs present perfect continuous.
cards.example: She's been seeing a physiotherapist since her injury.

cards.front: Fill in: When I arrived, they _____ (already/leave) the house.
cards.back: When I arrived, they had already left the house.
cards.meaning: The leaving happened before the arriving, an earlier past action, so past perfect is needed — Portuguese speakers often use simple past for both.
cards.example: By the time she called, he had already fixed the sink.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'When I got to the party, everyone already left.'
cards.back: When I got to the party, everyone had already left.
cards.meaning: One past action clearly precedes another, so the earlier one needs past perfect, not simple past.
cards.example: By the time we arrived, they had already cut the cake.

cards.front: Fill in: The bank _____ (already/close) my account by the time I called.
cards.back: The bank had already closed my account by the time I called.
cards.meaning: The closing occurred before the calling, an earlier past event, requiring past perfect.
cards.example: They had approved the loan before I even signed the papers.

cards.front: Translate: 'Quando ele me ligou, eu já tinha desligado o telefone.'
cards.back: When he called me, I had already turned off my phone.
cards.meaning: The turning off happened before the calling, so past perfect marks the earlier action.
cards.example: She had already read the message before I explained it.

cards.front: Fill in: By the time we got our coffee, it _____ (go) cold.
cards.back: By the time we got our coffee, it had gone cold.
cards.meaning: The cooling happened before 'getting the coffee,' an earlier past event, so past perfect is required.
cards.example: The café had already closed by the time we arrived.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (never/eat) Ethiopian food before that night.
cards.back: We had never eaten Ethiopian food before that night.
cards.meaning: An experience true up to a specific past moment uses past perfect, similar to present perfect but shifted to the past.
cards.example: I had never tried raw oysters before that dinner.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'When we got to the gate, the flight already left.'
cards.back: When we got to the gate, the flight had already left.
cards.meaning: The departure happened before arriving at the gate, so the earlier action needs past perfect.
cards.example: By the time we checked in, they had given away our seats.

cards.front: Fill in: She _____ (finish) the report before the meeting started.
cards.back: She had finished the report before the meeting started.
cards.meaning: The finishing precedes the starting of the meeting, an earlier past action requiring past perfect.
cards.example: He had submitted the proposal before the deadline passed.

cards.front: Fill in: The store _____ (sell out) of that model before I got there.
cards.back: The store had sold out of that model before I got there.
cards.meaning: The selling out happened before arriving, an earlier past event needing past perfect.
cards.example: They had already given away the last discount voucher.

cards.front: Fill in: By the time the ambulance arrived, the pain _____ (get) worse.
cards.back: By the time the ambulance arrived, the pain had gotten worse.
cards.meaning: The worsening happened progressively before the arrival, an earlier point, requiring past perfect.
cards.example: The doctor had already left when I got to the clinic.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'The plumber left before I noticed the leak.' (the leak was found after he left)
cards.back: The plumber had left before I noticed the leak.
cards.meaning: The plumber's leaving is the earlier of the two past events, so it takes past perfect.
cards.example: We had already painted the walls before we found the crack.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (not/meet) her husband before the wedding.
cards.back: I hadn't met her husband before the wedding.
cards.meaning: An action not yet completed before another past point uses past perfect negative.
cards.example: They hadn't seen each other in years before that reunion.

cards.front: Translate: 'Eu já tinha pago a conta quando recebi o aviso.'
cards.back: I had already paid the bill when I received the notice.
cards.meaning: The paying happened before receiving the notice, an earlier past action needing past perfect.
cards.example: She had already transferred the money before the bank called.

cards.front: Fill in: My battery _____ (die) before I could send the message.
cards.back: My battery had died before I could send the message.
cards.meaning: The dying happened before the failed attempt to send, an earlier past event.
cards.example: The app had already crashed before I saved my changes.

cards.front: Which tense expresses an action completed before another past action?
cards.back: Past perfect — e.g., 'The coffee had already cooled by the time I drank it.'
cards.meaning: Past perfect marks the earlier of two past events, something Portuguese often skips by using simple past for both.
cards.example: She had already left when the barista called her name.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I was full because I already ate a big lunch.'
cards.back: I was full because I had already eaten a big lunch.
cards.meaning: The eating precedes the feeling full, an earlier past action requiring past perfect.
cards.example: He felt sick because he had eaten too much dessert.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (book) the hotel months before the trip.
cards.back: We had booked the hotel months before the trip.
cards.meaning: The booking clearly precedes the trip, an earlier past action, so past perfect fits.
cards.example: They had planned the itinerary long before they packed.

cards.front: Fill in: By the time I joined the company, they _____ (already/change) the whole system.
cards.back: By the time I joined the company, they had already changed the whole system.
cards.meaning: The change happened before joining, the earlier of two past events.
cards.example: The team had already migrated the database before I started.

cards.front: Fill in: I realized I _____ (forget) my wallet at the checkout.
cards.back: I realized I had forgotten my wallet at the checkout.
cards.meaning: The forgetting happened before the realizing, an earlier past action needing past perfect.
cards.example: She noticed she had left her bag in the fitting room.

cards.front: Translate: 'Quando cheguei ao hospital, os sintomas já tinham piorado.'
cards.back: When I got to the hospital, the symptoms had already gotten worse.
cards.meaning: The worsening precedes arriving at the hospital, so past perfect marks the earlier action.
cards.example: The infection had already spread before they started treatment.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (renovate) the house for months before we finally moved in.
cards.back: We had been renovating the house for months before we finally moved in.
cards.meaning: An ongoing action before another past point, emphasizing duration, uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: He had been fixing the car for weeks before it finally started.

cards.front: Fill in: They _____ (date) for two years before they got engaged.
cards.back: They had been dating for two years before they got engaged.
cards.meaning: Duration of an action leading up to another past event uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: We had been planning the trip for months before we booked it.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (save) for a year before I finally bought the apartment.
cards.back: I had been saving for a year before I finally bought the apartment.
cards.meaning: Emphasis on the duration of an action before another past event uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: She had been investing for months before the market crashed.

cards.front: Fill in: My phone _____ (overheat) for days before it finally broke.
cards.back: My phone had been overheating for days before it finally broke.
cards.meaning: A continuous cause leading to a past result uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: The app had been crashing for weeks before they fixed it.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (work) there for five years before I opened my own café.
cards.back: I had been working there for five years before I opened my own café.
cards.meaning: Duration of a past action before a later past event uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: He had been roasting beans at home for years before he started the business.

cards.front: Translate: 'Nós estávamos esperando havia quarenta minutos quando finalmente nos sentaram.'
cards.back: We had been waiting for forty minutes when they finally seated us.
cards.meaning: Duration leading up to another past event requires past perfect continuous.
cards.example: They had been complaining for a while before the manager apologized.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (fly) for ten hours before we finally landed.
cards.back: We had been flying for ten hours before we finally landed.
cards.meaning: Ongoing duration before a past event uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: She had been traveling for two days before she reached home.

cards.front: Fill in: He _____ (negotiate) the contract for weeks before they signed it.
cards.back: He had been negotiating the contract for weeks before they signed it.
cards.meaning: Emphasis on the duration of the process before completion, in the past, uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: They had been discussing the merger for months before it happened.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (look) for that jacket for weeks before I finally found it on sale.
cards.back: I had been looking for that jacket for weeks before I finally found it on sale.
cards.meaning: Duration of the search before the successful past event uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: She had been hunting for a good deal for days before she bought the sofa.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (have) headaches for months before I saw a specialist.
cards.back: I had been having headaches for months before I saw a specialist.
cards.meaning: An ongoing symptom before a later past event uses past perfect continuous.
cards.example: He had been feeling weak for weeks before he was diagnosed.

cards.front: Fill in: Don't worry, I _____ (fix) the leak this weekend.
cards.back: Don't worry, I'll fix the leak this weekend.
cards.meaning: A spontaneous decision or promise made at the moment of speaking uses 'will'.
cards.example: I'll clean the garage tomorrow, I promise.

cards.front: Fill in: I think Marcos _____ (not/come) to the party tonight.
cards.back: I think Marcos won't come to the party tonight.
cards.meaning: A prediction based on opinion uses simple future with 'will'.
cards.example: I bet they'll love the surprise.

cards.front: Fill in: The teller said the transfer _____ (arrive) by tomorrow.
cards.back: The teller said the transfer will arrive by tomorrow.
cards.meaning: A prediction about a future event uses 'will'.
cards.example: Rates will probably go up next year.

cards.front: Fill in: Wait, my phone is ringing — I _____ (answer) it.
cards.back: Wait, my phone is ringing — I'll answer it.
cards.meaning: A spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking uses 'will'.
cards.example: I'll call you back in five minutes.

cards.front: Fill in: A: 'We're out of milk.' B: 'Okay, I _____ (get) some.'
cards.back: Okay, I'll get some.
cards.meaning: An instant decision made right at the moment of speaking uses 'will'.
cards.example: I'll grab an extra cup for you too.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (have) the salmon, please.
cards.back: I'll have the salmon, please.
cards.meaning: A decision made at the moment of ordering uses 'will'.
cards.example: I think I'll try the soup today.

cards.front: Fill in: According to the forecast, it _____ (rain) during our trip.
cards.back: According to the forecast, it will rain during our trip.
cards.meaning: A prediction based on evidence uses simple future with 'will'.
cards.example: The flight will probably be delayed because of the storm.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (send) you the file as soon as I finish.
cards.back: I'll send you the file as soon as I finish.
cards.meaning: A promise or spontaneous offer uses 'will'.
cards.example: She'll handle the client call this afternoon.

cards.front: Fill in: If it's too expensive, I just _____ (not/buy) it.
cards.back: If it's too expensive, I just won't buy it.
cards.meaning: A quick decision made on the spot uses 'will' (contracted as won't for negative).
cards.example: I'll wait for the sale instead.

cards.front: Fill in: The doctor said the results _____ (be) ready tomorrow.
cards.back: The doctor said the results will be ready tomorrow.
cards.meaning: A prediction about a future outcome uses 'will'.
cards.example: The swelling will probably go down in a few days.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (repaint) the living room next month — we already bought the paint.
cards.back: We're going to repaint the living room next month — we already bought the paint.
cards.meaning: A planned intention decided before speaking uses 'going to'.
cards.example: He's going to fix the fence next week.

cards.front: Fill in: Look at those clouds — it _____ (rain), so let's cancel the picnic.
cards.back: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain, so let's cancel the picnic.
cards.meaning: A prediction based on present evidence uses 'going to'.
cards.example: She's going to be late — she just texted me.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (open) a new account next week — I already filled out the form.
cards.back: I'm going to open a new account next week — I already filled out the form.
cards.meaning: A pre-decided plan uses 'going to,' not a spontaneous 'will'.
cards.example: They're going to raise the interest rate, according to the news.

cards.front: Fill in: My phone _____ (die) any second — look at the battery.
cards.back: My phone is going to die any second — look at the battery.
cards.meaning: A prediction based on visible present evidence uses 'going to'.
cards.example: The screen is going to crack if you drop it again.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (order) the same thing as always.
cards.back: I'm going to order the same thing as always.
cards.meaning: A pre-planned personal decision uses 'going to'.
cards.example: We're going to try the new seasonal drink.

cards.front: Fill in: We already booked the table — we _____ (celebrate) her promotion tonight.
cards.back: We already booked the table — we're going to celebrate her promotion tonight.
cards.meaning: A plan already arranged before speaking uses 'going to'.
cards.example: They're going to order the tasting menu.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (visit) Portugal in December — we already bought the tickets.
cards.back: We're going to visit Portugal in December — we already bought the tickets.
cards.meaning: A prior plan with evidence (tickets bought) uses 'going to'.
cards.example: He's going to backpack through South America next year.

cards.front: Fill in: The company _____ (launch) a new product next quarter.
cards.back: The company is going to launch a new product next quarter.
cards.meaning: A planned intention already decided within the organization uses 'going to'.
cards.example: They're going to hire two new developers.

cards.front: Fill in: This shirt is too small — I _____ (exchange) it.
cards.back: This shirt is too small — I'm going to exchange it.
cards.meaning: A decision already made based on present evidence uses 'going to'.
cards.example: She's going to return those shoes tomorrow.

cards.front: Fill in: The doctor said I _____ (need) surgery.
cards.back: The doctor said I'm going to need surgery.
cards.meaning: A planned or foreseen future event based on present evidence (a diagnosis) uses 'going to'.
cards.example: She's going to start physical therapy next week.

cards.front: Fill in: This time tomorrow, we _____ (paint) the bedroom.
cards.back: This time tomorrow, we'll be painting the bedroom.
cards.meaning: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future moment.
cards.example: By 6 p.m., he'll be mowing the lawn.

cards.front: Fill in: At 9 p.m., we _____ (still/celebrate) her birthday.
cards.back: At 9 p.m., we'll still be celebrating her birthday.
cards.meaning: An action expected to be in progress at a specific future time uses future continuous.
cards.example: This time next week, they'll be traveling to Rome.

cards.front: Fill in: Next Monday, the accountant _____ (review) our statements.
cards.back: Next Monday, the accountant will be reviewing our statements.
cards.meaning: An action in progress at a stated future point uses future continuous.
cards.example: By this time next month, I'll be making my last loan payment.

cards.front: Fill in: Don't call at 8 — I _____ (talk) to a client then.
cards.back: Don't call at 8 — I'll be talking to a client then.
cards.meaning: An action expected to be ongoing at a specific future time uses future continuous.
cards.example: At noon, she'll be presenting the new app.

cards.front: Fill in: At this time tomorrow, I _____ (relax) with a coffee on the porch.
cards.back: At this time tomorrow, I'll be relaxing with a coffee on the porch.
cards.meaning: Future continuous frames an action as ongoing at a future moment.
cards.example: By 8 a.m., the baristas will be opening the shop.

cards.front: Fill in: At 8 p.m. tonight, we _____ (eat) at that new steakhouse.
cards.back: At 8 p.m. tonight, we'll be eating at that new steakhouse.
cards.meaning: Describes an action expected to be happening at a specific future time.
cards.example: By then, the chef will be preparing the dessert course.

cards.front: Fill in: This time next week, we _____ (fly) over the Atlantic.
cards.back: This time next week, we'll be flying over the Atlantic.
cards.meaning: An action in progress at a specific future point uses future continuous.
cards.example: By Friday, we'll be exploring the old town.

cards.front: Fill in: At 10 tomorrow, I _____ (present) the quarterly results.
cards.back: At 10 tomorrow, I'll be presenting the quarterly results.
cards.meaning: An action planned to be in progress at a specific future time uses future continuous.
cards.example: This time next week, she'll be interviewing candidates.

cards.front: Fill in: By Friday, I _____ (spend) my whole paycheck on Christmas gifts.
cards.back: By Friday, I'll have spent my whole paycheck on Christmas gifts.
cards.meaning: Future perfect describes an action completed before a specific future point.
cards.example: By the end of the sale, they'll have sold out of that model.

cards.front: Fill in: By next month, I _____ (finish) the whole treatment.
cards.back: By next month, I'll have finished the whole treatment.
cards.meaning: An action expected to be completed before a future deadline uses future perfect.
cards.example: By the time you read this, the doctor will have called with the results.

cards.front: Fill in: By the time you get home, I _____ (fix) the sink.
cards.back: By the time you get home, I'll have fixed the sink.
cards.meaning: An action that will be completed before another future event uses future perfect.
cards.example: By next summer, we'll have finished renovating the whole house.

cards.front: Fill in: By midnight, they _____ (already/leave) the party.
cards.back: By midnight, they'll have already left the party.
cards.meaning: An action completed before a specific future time uses future perfect.
cards.example: By the time we arrive, the guests will have eaten all the cake.

cards.front: Fill in: By 2030, I _____ (pay off) my mortgage.
cards.back: By 2030, I'll have paid off my mortgage.
cards.meaning: An action completed before a stated future point uses future perfect.
cards.example: By next year, she'll have saved enough for a down payment.

cards.front: Fill in: By tonight, I _____ (send) at least fifty messages about this project.
cards.back: By tonight, I'll have sent at least fifty messages about this project.
cards.meaning: An action viewed as complete by a future point uses future perfect.
cards.example: By the end of the day, he'll have answered every email.

cards.front: Fill in: By the time you arrive, I _____ (already/finish) my coffee.
cards.back: By the time you arrive, I'll have already finished my coffee.
cards.meaning: Completion before another future event uses future perfect.
cards.example: By 9 a.m., they'll have served hundreds of customers.

cards.front: Fill in: By the time dessert comes, we _____ (be) here for two hours.
cards.back: By the time dessert comes, we'll have been here for two hours.
cards.meaning: Future perfect marks a duration viewed as complete by a stated future point.
cards.example: By closing time, the restaurant will have served its last table.

cards.front: Fill in: If you _____ (not/have) a visa, they _____ (not/let) you in.
cards.back: If you don't have a visa, they don't let you in.
cards.meaning: Zero conditional expresses a general truth or rule, always true.
cards.example: If your passport expires, you can't board the plane.

cards.front: Fill in: If the server _____ (crash), the whole office _____ (lose) internet.
cards.back: If the server crashes, the whole office loses internet.
cards.meaning: A general, always-true cause-and-effect uses zero conditional.
cards.example: If you don't clock in, the system flags you as absent.

cards.front: Fill in: If you _____ (pay) in cash, the store _____ (give) a discount.
cards.back: If you pay in cash, the store gives a discount.
cards.meaning: A general rule or fact uses present simple in both clauses.
cards.example: If an item is defective, they replace it for free.

cards.front: Fill in: If you _____ (skip) meals, your blood sugar _____ (drop).
cards.back: If you skip meals, your blood sugar drops.
cards.meaning: A scientific or general fact uses zero conditional.
cards.example: If you don't sleep enough, your immune system weakens.

cards.front: Fill in: If water _____ (freeze), it _____ (expand).
cards.back: If water freezes, it expands.
cards.meaning: A universal scientific fact uses zero conditional.
cards.example: If you overload the outlet, the breaker trips.

cards.front: Fill in: If you _____ (arrive) late to Marina's parties, she _____ (get) upset.
cards.back: If you arrive late to Marina's parties, she gets upset.
cards.meaning: A general pattern or habit true every time uses zero conditional.
cards.example: If you forget her birthday, she never lets it go.

cards.front: Fill in: If your balance _____ (go) below zero, the bank _____ (charge) a fee.
cards.back: If your balance goes below zero, the bank charges a fee.
cards.meaning: A fixed rule or policy uses zero conditional.
cards.example: If you miss a payment, your credit score drops.

cards.front: Fill in: If the battery _____ (get) too hot, the phone _____ (shut) down automatically.
cards.back: If the battery gets too hot, the phone shuts down automatically.
cards.meaning: A general technical fact uses zero conditional.
cards.example: If you drop your phone in water, it usually stops working.

cards.front: Fill in: If they _____ (be) out of oat milk, I _____ (just/get) regular milk.
cards.back: If they're out of oat milk, I'll just get regular milk.
cards.meaning: A real, possible future situation uses first conditional: present simple + will.
cards.example: If the line is too long, we'll go somewhere else.

cards.front: Fill in: If we _____ (not/book) a table, we _____ (have) to wait.
cards.back: If we don't book a table, we'll have to wait.
cards.meaning: A likely future condition and its result use first conditional.
cards.example: If the soup is too spicy, I'll ask for something else.

cards.front: Fill in: If our flight _____ (be) delayed, we _____ (miss) the connection.
cards.back: If our flight is delayed, we'll miss the connection.
cards.meaning: A realistic future possibility uses first conditional.
cards.example: If it rains tomorrow, we'll postpone the hike.

cards.front: Fill in: If you _____ (finish) the report early, I _____ (review) it today.
cards.back: If you finish the report early, I'll review it today.
cards.meaning: A real, likely condition about the future uses first conditional.
cards.example: If the client agrees, we'll sign the contract this week.

cards.front: Fill in: If the jacket _____ (not/fit), I _____ (return) it.
cards.back: If the jacket doesn't fit, I'll return it.
cards.meaning: A realistic possible future situation uses first conditional.
cards.example: If there's a sale next week, I'll wait to buy it.

cards.front: Fill in: If the pain _____ (get) worse, I _____ (go) to the ER.
cards.back: If the pain gets worse, I'll go to the ER.
cards.meaning: A real possible future scenario and its consequence use first conditional.
cards.example: If the fever doesn't go down, we'll call the doctor.

cards.front: Fill in: If the plumber _____ (not/come) today, we _____ (call) someone else.
cards.back: If the plumber doesn't come today, we'll call someone else.
cards.meaning: A likely future condition uses first conditional.
cards.example: If it keeps leaking, we'll need a new pipe.

cards.front: Fill in: If Lucas _____ (invite) us, we _____ (definitely/go).
cards.back: If Lucas invites us, we'll definitely go.
cards.meaning: A realistic future possibility uses first conditional.
cards.example: If she's free on Saturday, we'll meet for lunch.

cards.front: Fill in: If the transfer _____ (not/arrive) by tomorrow, I _____ (call) the bank.
cards.back: If the transfer doesn't arrive by tomorrow, I'll call the bank.
cards.meaning: A real possible future situation uses first conditional.
cards.example: If they charge me twice, I'll dispute it.

cards.front: Fill in: If my phone _____ (break) again, I _____ (buy) a new one.
cards.back: If my phone breaks again, I'll buy a new one.
cards.meaning: A likely, real future condition uses first conditional.
cards.example: If the update fixes the bug, I'll be relieved.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (own) a café, I _____ (serve) only fair-trade coffee.
cards.back: If I owned a café, I would serve only fair-trade coffee.
cards.meaning: An unreal, hypothetical present situation uses second conditional: past simple + would — not 'will' as some learners mistakenly use.
cards.example: If I had more time, I would learn how to make latte art.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'If I would have more money, I would eat here every week.'
cards.back: If I had more money, I would eat here every week.
cards.meaning: Using 'would' in the if-clause is a common Portuguese-transfer error; second conditional needs past simple in the if-clause.
cards.example: If this place were cheaper, we would come more often.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (speak) fluent Italian, traveling around Italy _____ (be) so much easier.
cards.back: If I spoke fluent Italian, traveling around Italy would be so much easier.
cards.meaning: A hypothetical, unreal present situation uses second conditional.
cards.example: If we had a car, we would explore the countryside.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (be) the manager, I _____ (change) the whole schedule.
cards.back: If I were the manager, I would change the whole schedule.
cards.meaning: Second conditional uses 'were' for all subjects in formal hypothetical statements, expressing an unreal present.
cards.example: If she worked harder, she would get promoted.

cards.front: Translate: 'Se eu tivesse dinheiro agora, compraria esse casaco.'
cards.back: If I had money now, I would buy this coat.
cards.meaning: An unreal present condition uses second conditional, unlike the subjunctive Portuguese uses naturally.
cards.example: If it were on sale, I would buy two.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (have) better health insurance, I _____ (see) a specialist right away.
cards.back: If I had better health insurance, I would see a specialist right away.
cards.meaning: An unreal, hypothetical present situation uses second conditional.
cards.example: If the clinic were closer, I would go more often.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'If I would have a bigger kitchen, I would cook every day.'
cards.back: If I had a bigger kitchen, I would cook every day.
cards.meaning: The if-clause never takes 'would' in second conditional — a frequent mistake from Portuguese speakers.
cards.example: If we owned this house, we would renovate the attic.

cards.front: Fill in: If Marina _____ (not/be) so busy, she _____ (come) to more parties.
cards.back: If Marina weren't so busy, she would come to more parties.
cards.meaning: An unreal present situation and its hypothetical result use second conditional.
cards.example: If he lived closer, we would hang out more often.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (win) the lottery, I _____ (pay off) all my debts immediately.
cards.back: If I won the lottery, I would pay off all my debts immediately.
cards.meaning: A hypothetical, unlikely present or future scenario uses second conditional.
cards.example: If interest rates were lower, more people would invest.

cards.front: Fill in: If my phone _____ (not/be) so old, it _____ (not/crash) all the time.
cards.back: If my phone weren't so old, it wouldn't crash all the time.
cards.meaning: An unreal present condition and consequence use second conditional.
cards.example: If I had a better plan, I would use more data.

cards.front: Which tense expresses an unreal, hypothetical situation in the present or future?
cards.back: Second conditional — e.g., 'If I had my own café, I would design the menu myself.'
cards.meaning: Second conditional imagines a present or future situation contrary to reality.
cards.example: If she weren't allergic, she would order the cappuccino with milk.

cards.front: Fill in: If this restaurant _____ (have) live music, I _____ (come) every weekend.
cards.back: If this restaurant had live music, I would come every weekend.
cards.meaning: An imagined, unreal present situation uses second conditional.
cards.example: If they served brunch, we would visit on Sundays.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'If I would know the language, I would travel alone.'
cards.back: If I knew the language, I would travel alone.
cards.meaning: 'Would' cannot appear in the if-clause; this is a classic transfer error from Portuguese.
cards.example: If I had more vacation days, I would visit more countries.

cards.front: Fill in: If we _____ (have) more staff, we _____ (finish) the project faster.
cards.back: If we had more staff, we would finish the project faster.
cards.meaning: An unreal present situation and its imagined result use second conditional.
cards.example: If the software worked better, we would save hours every week.

cards.front: Fill in: If this store _____ (accept) installments, I _____ (buy) it right now.
cards.back: If this store accepted installments, I would buy it right now.
cards.meaning: A hypothetical present condition uses second conditional.
cards.example: If they had my size, I would try it on.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/be) afraid of needles, this _____ (not/be) so stressful.
cards.back: If I weren't afraid of needles, this wouldn't be so stressful.
cards.meaning: An unreal present state and its hypothetical effect use second conditional.
cards.example: If the waiting room were quieter, I would feel calmer.

cards.front: Fill in: If we _____ (call) a plumber sooner, the pipe _____ (not/burst).
cards.back: If we had called a plumber sooner, the pipe wouldn't have burst.
cards.meaning: An unreal past condition and its unreal past result use third conditional — 'had + past participle' plus 'would have + past participle'.
cards.example: If they had fixed the roof earlier, it wouldn't have leaked during the storm.

cards.front: Translate: 'Se eu tivesse sabido, teria ligado.'
cards.back: If I had known, I would have called.
cards.meaning: Third conditional expresses a hypothetical past that didn't happen — Portuguese expresses this more simply, so the double 'had...would have' structure is often lost.
cards.example: If she had told me earlier, I would have come to the party.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (check) my balance, I _____ (not/overdraft) my account.
cards.back: If I had checked my balance, I wouldn't have overdrafted my account.
cards.meaning: An unreal past condition and consequence use third conditional.
cards.example: If they had warned me about the fee, I wouldn't have made the transfer.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (charge) my phone last night, it _____ (not/die) during the call.
cards.back: If I had charged my phone last night, it wouldn't have died during the call.
cards.meaning: An unreal past situation with a hypothetical past result uses third conditional.
cards.example: If she had backed up her photos, she wouldn't have lost them.

cards.front: Fill in: If the barista _____ (hear) my order correctly, I _____ (not/get) the wrong drink.
cards.back: If the barista had heard my order correctly, I wouldn't have gotten the wrong drink.
cards.meaning: Third conditional imagines a different past outcome that never happened.
cards.example: If they had opened earlier, we wouldn't have missed our train.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'If I would have known it was so expensive, I wouldn't have ordered it.'
cards.back: If I had known it was so expensive, I wouldn't have ordered it.
cards.meaning: The if-clause needs 'had + past participle,' not 'would have,' a very common error for Portuguese speakers.
cards.example: If we had read the reviews, we wouldn't have chosen that place.

cards.front: Fill in: If we _____ (arrive) earlier, we _____ (not/miss) the flight.
cards.back: If we had arrived earlier, we wouldn't have missed the flight.
cards.meaning: An unreal past condition and its unreal past consequence require third conditional.
cards.example: If I had packed the night before, I wouldn't have forgotten my charger.

cards.front: Fill in: If she _____ (send) the email sooner, the client _____ (not/cancel) the deal.
cards.back: If she had sent the email sooner, the client wouldn't have cancelled the deal.
cards.meaning: Third conditional expresses a hypothetical alternative to a past event that actually happened.
cards.example: If we had prepared better, the presentation would have gone smoothly.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (see) the price tag, I _____ (not/pick) it up.
cards.back: If I had seen the price tag, I wouldn't have picked it up.
cards.meaning: An imagined different past uses third conditional.
cards.example: If they had had my size, I would have bought two.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (go) to the doctor sooner, the infection _____ (not/get) so bad.
cards.back: If I had gone to the doctor sooner, the infection wouldn't have gotten so bad.
cards.meaning: Third conditional imagines a different past outcome for a past mistake.
cards.example: If she had taken the medicine on time, she would have recovered faster.

cards.front: Translate: 'Se tivéssemos consertado a torneira, não teríamos gasto tanta água.'
cards.back: If we had fixed the faucet, we wouldn't have wasted so much water.
cards.meaning: The double past-perfect plus would-have structure of third conditional has no direct Portuguese equivalent.
cards.example: If he had checked the wiring, the lights wouldn't have gone out.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (know) about the surprise party, I _____ (act) differently.
cards.back: If I had known about the surprise party, I would have acted differently.
cards.meaning: An unreal past condition and imagined result use third conditional.
cards.example: If they had invited us, we would have gone.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'If the bank would have told me, I would have paid on time.'
cards.back: If the bank had told me, I would have paid on time.
cards.meaning: 'Would have' cannot go in the if-clause; only 'had + past participle' belongs there.
cards.example: If I had read the fine print, I wouldn't have signed up for that fee.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/drop) my phone, the screen _____ (not/crack).
cards.back: If I hadn't dropped my phone, the screen wouldn't have cracked.
cards.meaning: A negative unreal past condition and result use third conditional.
cards.example: If she hadn't updated the app, it wouldn't have crashed.

cards.front: Fill in: If they _____ (not/run out) of beans, we _____ (get) our usual order.
cards.back: If they hadn't run out of beans, we would have gotten our usual order.
cards.meaning: Third conditional describes an unreal alternative to something that already happened and can't be changed.
cards.example: If the machine hadn't broken, the line wouldn't have been so long.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/eat) so much at lunch, I _____ (be) hungry now.
cards.back: If I hadn't eaten so much at lunch, I would be hungry now.
cards.meaning: Mixed conditional: an unreal past condition (past perfect) produces a present result (would + base verb).
cards.example: If she hadn't skipped breakfast, she wouldn't be so tired now.

cards.front: Fill in: If we _____ (book) the flight earlier, we _____ (be) in Rome right now.
cards.back: If we had booked the flight earlier, we would be in Rome right now.
cards.meaning: An unreal past action affects a hypothetical present state — a mixed conditional with no direct Portuguese equivalent.
cards.example: If he had applied for the visa in time, he would be traveling with us now.

cards.front: Fill in: If she _____ (not/quit) her job, she _____ (be) the manager today.
cards.back: If she hadn't quit her job, she would be the manager today.
cards.meaning: A past unreal condition leads to a present hypothetical result — mixed conditional.
cards.example: If we had hired more staff last year, we wouldn't be so overwhelmed now.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (invest) back then, I _____ (be) rich today.
cards.back: If I had invested back then, I would be rich today.
cards.meaning: The condition is in the past (had invested), but the result is in the present (would be) — mixed conditional.
cards.example: If they hadn't raised the fees, more people would use this bank.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/lose) my old phone, I _____ (still/have) those photos.
cards.back: If I hadn't lost my old phone, I would still have those photos.
cards.meaning: A past unreal event with a present consequence uses mixed conditional.
cards.example: If she had backed up her contacts, she wouldn't be starting from zero now.

cards.front: Fill in: If he _____ (not/open) that café five years ago, he _____ (not/be) so successful now.
cards.back: If he hadn't opened that café five years ago, he wouldn't be so successful now.
cards.meaning: A past condition (third conditional style) produces a present result (second conditional style) — that's a mixed conditional.
cards.example: If she hadn't learned to roast coffee, she wouldn't be running her own brand now.

cards.front: Fill in: If we _____ (buy) this house last year, we _____ (still/pay) less in interest.
cards.back: If we had bought this house last year, we would still be paying less in interest.
cards.meaning: An unreal past action shapes a present ongoing situation, requiring a mixed conditional.
cards.example: If they had insulated the attic, the house wouldn't be so cold now.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/move) abroad, I _____ (still/see) my friends every week.
cards.back: If I hadn't moved abroad, I would still see my friends every week.
cards.meaning: A past unreal decision has present consequences — a classic mixed conditional.
cards.example: If she hadn't lost touch with him, they would still be close now.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (take) my medication properly, I _____ (feel) better now.
cards.back: If I had taken my medication properly, I would feel better now.
cards.meaning: The unreal condition is past, but the result is present — mixed conditional.
cards.example: If he hadn't ignored the symptoms, he wouldn't be so sick now.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/spend) so much last month, I _____ (be able) to afford this now.
cards.back: If I hadn't spent so much last month, I would be able to afford this now.
cards.meaning: A past unreal action affects a hypothetical present ability — mixed conditional.
cards.example: If she had saved more, she would be shopping without worry now.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (be) more organized, I _____ (not/miss) that connection yesterday.
cards.back: If I were more organized, I wouldn't have missed that connection yesterday.
cards.meaning: This is the reverse mixed conditional: a present unreal characteristic explains a past result.
cards.example: If he weren't so careless, he wouldn't have lost his passport last week.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (not/be) so shy, I _____ (speak up) in yesterday's meeting.
cards.back: If I weren't so shy, I would have spoken up in yesterday's meeting.
cards.meaning: A general present trait (unreal) leads to a hypothetical different past action — mixed conditional.
cards.example: If she weren't so busy in general, she would have joined us last night.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (be) better with money, I _____ (not/max out) my credit card last month.
cards.back: If I were better with money, I wouldn't have maxed out my credit card last month.
cards.meaning: A present unreal trait explains a specific past mistake — mixed conditional.
cards.example: If he weren't so impulsive, he wouldn't have overdrafted last week.

cards.front: Fill in: If I _____ (be) more tech-savvy, I _____ (not/lose) all my data yesterday.
cards.back: If I were more tech-savvy, I wouldn't have lost all my data yesterday.
cards.meaning: A general present characteristic (unreal) shapes a hypothetical past outcome.
cards.example: If she weren't so forgetful, she wouldn't have left her phone at the restaurant last night.

cards.front: Which structure combines a past unreal condition with a present hypothetical result, or vice versa?
cards.back: Mixed conditional — e.g., 'If we had fixed the roof, we wouldn't be dealing with this mess now.'
cards.meaning: Mixed conditionals connect two different time frames, something that doesn't exist as a fixed structure in Portuguese.
cards.example: If he were more careful, he wouldn't have broken the window last week.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): This coffee _____ (grow) in Colombia.
cards.back: This coffee is grown in Colombia.
cards.meaning: Simple present passive focuses on the process rather than who does it.
cards.example: These beans are roasted locally.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The dish _____ (prepare) fresh every morning.
cards.back: The dish is prepared fresh every morning.
cards.meaning: A general routine described from the receiver's perspective uses present simple passive.
cards.example: The bread is baked in-house.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): My luggage _____ (lose) somewhere between connections.
cards.back: My luggage was lost somewhere between connections.
cards.meaning: A finished past action affecting the subject uses simple past passive.
cards.example: Our passports were checked twice at the gate.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The report _____ (submit) by Friday.
cards.back: The report will be submitted by Friday.
cards.meaning: A future action, with focus on the report rather than who submits it, uses future simple passive.
cards.example: The new policy will be announced next week.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): This item _____ (already/sell) — sorry.
cards.back: This item has already been sold — sorry.
cards.meaning: A past action with present relevance, focused on the item, uses present perfect passive.
cards.example: All the tickets have been reserved.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The results _____ (send) to your doctor by the time you get home.
cards.back: The results will have been sent to your doctor by the time you get home.
cards.meaning: Future perfect passive describes an action completed before a future point, focused on the receiver.
cards.example: The prescription will have been filled by tomorrow morning.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The kitchen _____ (renovate) right now.
cards.back: The kitchen is being renovated right now.
cards.meaning: Present continuous passive describes an action in progress now, focused on the object.
cards.example: The carpet is being cleaned as we speak.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The invitations _____ (send) out last week.
cards.back: The invitations were sent out last week.
cards.meaning: A finished past action, focused on the invitations rather than who sent them, uses simple past passive.
cards.example: The venue was booked months in advance.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): Your application _____ (review) at the moment.
cards.back: Your application is being reviewed at the moment.
cards.meaning: An ongoing action right now, seen from the object's perspective, uses present continuous passive.
cards.example: Your card is being processed.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The software update _____ (install) automatically last night.
cards.back: The software update was installed automatically last night.
cards.meaning: A completed past action focused on the update, not the agent, uses simple past passive.
cards.example: The app was downloaded over a million times.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'The coffee is serve with milk.'
cards.back: The coffee is served with milk.
cards.meaning: Passive voice requires 'be' plus the past participle, not the base form.
cards.example: The pastries are baked fresh daily.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): By the time we arrived, the table _____ (already/give) to someone else.
cards.back: By the time we arrived, the table had already been given to someone else.
cards.meaning: Past perfect passive marks an action completed before another past event, focused on the table.
cards.example: The reservation had been cancelled before we called.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): New security rules _____ (introduce) since last year.
cards.back: New security rules have been introduced since last year.
cards.meaning: Present perfect passive links a past change to its present relevance.
cards.example: Extra checks have been added at that airport.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The meeting room _____ (book) for the whole afternoon.
cards.back: The meeting room is booked for the whole afternoon.
cards.meaning: A present state resulting from an action, described passively, uses simple present passive.
cards.example: The contract is signed by both parties.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): These shoes _____ (make) by hand.
cards.back: These shoes are made by hand.
cards.meaning: A general fact about a process uses simple present passive.
cards.example: This jewelry is designed locally.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): I _____ (examine) by three different doctors last week.
cards.back: I was examined by three different doctors last week.
cards.meaning: A completed past action affecting the patient, with the agent mentioned, uses simple past passive.
cards.example: The samples were tested at the lab.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The new sofa _____ (deliver) tomorrow afternoon.
cards.back: The new sofa will be delivered tomorrow afternoon.
cards.meaning: A planned future action, focused on the sofa, uses future simple passive.
cards.example: The fence will be repaired next week.

cards.front: Fill in (passive): The transaction _____ (not/process) yet.
cards.back: The transaction hasn't been processed yet.
cards.meaning: Present perfect passive expresses an unfinished situation up to now, focused on the transaction.
cards.example: The refund hasn't been issued yet.

cards.front: Translate: 'Eu mandei consertar a máquina de café.'
cards.back: I had the coffee machine fixed.
cards.meaning: Causative form ('have something done') expresses that someone else performed the action for you — Portuguese usually just says 'I fixed' even when someone else did it.
cards.example: She had the espresso machine cleaned professionally.

cards.front: Fill in: The owner _____ (the kitchen/renovate) last month.
cards.back: The owner had the kitchen renovated last month.
cards.meaning: Causative form shows the owner arranged for someone else to do the work.
cards.example: They got the menu redesigned by a professional.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I did my passport photos at a shop.'
cards.back: I had my passport photos taken at a shop.
cards.meaning: When someone else performs a service for you, English uses the causative 'have something done,' not a direct action verb.
cards.example: We got our visas processed before the trip.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (the contract/review) by a lawyer before signing.
cards.back: We had the contract reviewed by a lawyer before signing.
cards.meaning: Causative form shows the action was done by someone else on the subject's behalf.
cards.example: They got the presentation translated into English.

cards.front: Translate: 'Vou mandar ajustar essa calça.'
cards.back: I'm going to have these pants altered.
cards.meaning: The causative form is required because a tailor, not the speaker, performs the alteration.
cards.example: She's going to get her ring resized.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (my teeth/clean) at the dentist yesterday.
cards.back: I had my teeth cleaned at the dentist yesterday.
cards.meaning: The dentist performs the action, so causative 'have something done' is required, not 'I cleaned my teeth' as Portuguese speakers often say directly.
cards.example: He had his eyes tested last week.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (the roof/repair) after the storm.
cards.back: We had the roof repaired after the storm.
cards.meaning: Causative form is used because a professional, not the homeowner, did the repair.
cards.example: They got the carpets replaced last year.

cards.front: Fill in: For her birthday, she _____ (a cake/deliver) to the office.
cards.back: For her birthday, she had a cake delivered to the office.
cards.meaning: Someone arranged for a service to happen, requiring causative form.
cards.example: They got the flowers sent as a surprise.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I made translate my documents for the loan application.'
cards.back: I had my documents translated for the loan application.
cards.meaning: 'Had something done' is the correct causative structure, not 'made translate,' a common mix-up.
cards.example: She got her credit report checked before applying.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (my screen/replace) after I dropped it.
cards.back: I had my screen replaced after I dropped it.
cards.meaning: The repair shop performed the action, requiring causative form.
cards.example: He got his phone unlocked at a small shop.

cards.front: Fill in: They _____ (the espresso machine/service) every six months.
cards.back: They have the espresso machine serviced every six months.
cards.meaning: A recurring arrangement where someone else performs the service uses causative form.
cards.example: We get our water filters changed regularly.

cards.front: Translate: 'O restaurante mandou pintar a fachada.'
cards.back: The restaurant had the front painted.
cards.meaning: Causative form marks that a painter, not the restaurant staff, did the work.
cards.example: They got the sign replaced last week.

cards.front: Fill in: We _____ (our bags/inspect) at customs.
cards.back: We had our bags inspected at customs.
cards.meaning: Someone else (customs officers) performed the action on the subject's belongings, requiring causative form.
cards.example: They got their tickets upgraded at the counter.

cards.front: Fill in: She _____ (her badge/reissue) after losing the old one.
cards.back: She had her badge reissued after losing the old one.
cards.meaning: The company, not the employee, performed the reissuing, requiring causative form.
cards.example: We got the office repainted over the weekend.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (the watch/engrave) as a gift.
cards.back: I had the watch engraved as a gift.
cards.meaning: A jeweler performed the engraving, requiring the causative structure.
cards.example: She got her shoes polished before the interview.

cards.front: Fill in: I need to _____ (my blood/test) next week.
cards.back: I need to have my blood tested next week.
cards.meaning: A lab technician performs the test, not the patient, so causative form is required.
cards.example: He's going to have his knee scanned tomorrow.

cards.front: Report: Ana said, 'I love this new blend.'
cards.back: Ana said she loved that new blend.
cards.meaning: Reported speech shifts present to past ('love' to 'loved') and 'this' to 'that' — backshifting that Portuguese speakers often skip.
cards.example: He said he preferred espresso over filter coffee.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'She said she is not hungry.' (reported later)
cards.back: She said she wasn't hungry.
cards.meaning: Reported speech requires the verb to shift back a tense, from present to past.
cards.example: He told us he didn't like spicy food.

cards.front: Report: The agent said, 'Your flight will be delayed.'
cards.back: The agent said our flight would be delayed.
cards.meaning: 'Will' shifts to 'would' in reported speech, matching the past reporting verb.
cards.example: She told me the train would leave from a different platform.

cards.front: Report: My boss said, 'I have finished the review.'
cards.back: My boss said he had finished the review.
cards.meaning: Present perfect shifts to past perfect in reported speech.
cards.example: She said she had already sent the invoice.

cards.front: Report: The clerk said, 'We don't accept returns without a receipt.'
cards.back: The clerk said they didn't accept returns without a receipt.
cards.meaning: Simple present shifts to simple past in reported statements.
cards.example: He said the store closed at nine.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'The doctor said I am fine.'
cards.back: The doctor said I was fine.
cards.meaning: Reported speech backshifts present to past, an error learners commonly skip because Portuguese doesn't always require this.
cards.example: She told me the results were normal.

cards.front: Report: The plumber said, 'I can fix it tomorrow.'
cards.back: The plumber said he could fix it tomorrow.
cards.meaning: 'Can' shifts to 'could' in reported speech.
cards.example: He said he would come back next week.

cards.front: Report: Bianca said, 'I'm going to the party tonight.'
cards.back: Bianca said she was going to the party that night.
cards.meaning: Present continuous shifts to past continuous, and time expressions also change ('tonight' becomes 'that night').
cards.example: He said he was leaving early the next day.

cards.front: Report: The manager said, 'We charged you twice by mistake.'
cards.back: The manager said they had charged me twice by mistake.
cards.meaning: Simple past shifts to past perfect in reported speech, marking an even earlier past event.
cards.example: She told me the transfer had already gone through.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'He told me he is busy right now.'
cards.back: He told me he was busy right then.
cards.meaning: Present tense and time references shift when reporting speech from the past.
cards.example: She said she couldn't talk at that moment.

cards.front: Report: The barista said, 'I made your order wrong.'
cards.back: The barista said she had made my order wrong.
cards.meaning: Simple past in direct speech shifts to past perfect in reported speech.
cards.example: He admitted he had forgotten the sugar.

cards.front: Report: The waiter said, 'The kitchen is closing soon.'
cards.back: The waiter said the kitchen was closing soon.
cards.meaning: Present continuous backshifts to past continuous in reported speech.
cards.example: She said the special was running out.

cards.front: Report: My friend said, 'I will pick you up at the airport.'
cards.back: My friend said she would pick me up at the airport.
cards.meaning: 'Will' shifts to 'would', and pronouns also change to match the reporter's perspective.
cards.example: He said he would text me when he landed.

cards.front: Report: The client said, 'I haven't received the invoice.'
cards.back: The client said she hadn't received the invoice.
cards.meaning: Present perfect shifts to past perfect when reporting speech.
cards.example: He said he hadn't approved the changes yet.

cards.front: Report: The cashier said, 'This discount ends today.'
cards.back: The cashier said the discount ended that day.
cards.meaning: Present simple shifts to past simple, and 'today' shifts to 'that day'.
cards.example: She said the sale started the following week.

cards.front: Report: The nurse said, 'You should rest for a few days.'
cards.back: The nurse said I should rest for a few days.
cards.meaning: 'Should' does not change form in reported speech, but the pronoun still shifts.
cards.example: The doctor said I shouldn't lift heavy things.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (should/call) the plumber sooner — the leak got much worse.
cards.back: I should have called the plumber sooner — the leak got much worse.
cards.meaning: 'Should have' expresses regret about a past action that wasn't done.
cards.example: We should have fixed the roof before winter.

cards.front: Fill in: She _____ (could/come) to the party, but she chose to stay home.
cards.back: She could have come to the party, but she chose to stay home.
cards.meaning: 'Could have' expresses an unrealized past possibility.
cards.example: They could have joined us, but they were too tired.

cards.front: Find and fix the error: 'I should call the bank yesterday.'
cards.back: I should have called the bank yesterday.
cards.meaning: Regret about a past action requires 'should have,' not just 'should' — learners often drop 'have'.
cards.example: You should have checked the exchange rate before transferring.

cards.front: Fill in: He _____ (must/lose) his phone somewhere on the bus.
cards.back: He must have lost his phone somewhere on the bus.
cards.meaning: 'Must have' expresses a strong logical deduction about the past.
cards.example: She must have forgotten to charge it overnight.

cards.front: Fill in: I _____ (would/order) the same thing, honestly.
cards.back: I would have ordered the same thing, honestly.
cards.meaning: 'Would have' expresses a hypothetical past action, imagining what one would have done.
cards.example: He would have tried the new blend if he'd had time.

cards.front: Translate: 'Eu deveria ter pedido a sobremesa.'
cards.back: I should have ordered the dessert.
